p: I must declare an interest. I have met Mr Charles Darwin twice, once at a dinner in London in the eighteen-forties, when he was known chiefly as the author of an agreeable book of travels, and once, some years after his great book appeared, at the house of a mutual friend, when he was unwell, as he generally is, and spoke very little. I found him modest, courteous and kind, the least revolutionary-looking man I ever saw. He has done more to unsettle the beliefs of my generation than any man since Copernicus.

Charles Darwin was born in eighteen hundred and nine, at Shrewsbury, in my own county, the son of a prosperous physician and grandson both of Erasmus Darwin, a physician, poet and early speculator on the transformation of species, and of Josiah Wedgwood the potter. He was sent to Edinburgh to study medicine, and fled from the operating theatre, where surgery was then performed without anaesthetic; then to Cambridge, to prepare to become a clergyman, where he spent most of his time collecting beetles. In eighteen thirty-one, at the age of twenty-two, he was offered a place as gentleman companion to the captain of His Majesty's Ship Beagle, which was to survey the coasts of South America. The voyage lasted nearly five years and took him round the world.

He saw the fossils of enormous extinct animals in the rocks of Argentina, curiously like the living sloths and armadillos of the same region. He felt an earthquake in Chile and saw the land raised several feet by it, and understood how mountains might be lifted over ages. And in the Galápagos Islands, in the Pacific off the coast of Ecuador, he collected birds, tortoises and plants that differed from island to island, as though each island had its own varieties, descended, perhaps, from some common ancestor that had come from the mainland. It was the mockingbirds, more than the famous finches, that first set him thinking.

Back in England, he married his cousin Emma Wedgwood, settled at Down House in Kent, became an invalid, and worked. In eighteen thirty-eight, reading for amusement the Essay on the Principle of Population of the Reverend Thomas Malthus, which argues that populations tend always to grow faster than their food, so that most creatures born must die young, he saw how species might change. Among the many offspring of any creature, there are always small differences. Those whose differences happen to suit them a little better to their circumstances are a little more likely to survive and to have offspring of their own, and to pass on those differences. Over immense spans of time, the accumulation of such small advantages could change one species into another, or divide one into many. He called this natural selection, by analogy with the selection practised by breeders of pigeons, dogs and cattle, which he studied minutely.

He wrote it down in eighteen forty-two, enlarged it in eighteen forty-four, gave instructions to his wife for its publication if he died, and then, for nearly twenty years, did not publish it. He spent eight of those years writing about barnacles. He knew what storms the theory would raise, and he wished to make it unanswerable. In eighteen fifty-eight he received a letter from a young naturalist collecting in the Malay Archipelago, Alfred Russel Wallace, enclosing an essay that set out, independently, almost exactly the same theory. Darwin's friends, Sir Charles Lyell and Joseph Hooker, arranged for the two papers to be read together at the Linnean Society, and Darwin hurried out what he called an abstract of his great work: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, published in November eighteen fifty-nine. The first printing sold out to the booksellers on the day of publication.

It was not the idea of evolution that was new; that had been proposed before, by Lamarck in France and in an anonymous English book of eighteen forty-four called Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, which, I may say, I read in my college and thought very foolish. What was new was the mechanism, and the enormous weight of evidence with which Darwin supported it. Natural selection required no design and no designer. The beautiful adaptations of living things, the eye, the wing, the hand, which Archdeacon Paley had held up as the clearest proof of a wise Creator, could arise, Darwin said, from the blind sifting of chance variations over immeasurable time.

The famous debate at Oxford in June eighteen-sixty, at the meeting of the British Association, between Bishop Samuel Wilberforce and Professor Thomas Huxley, I witnessed from the back of a very crowded room. The bishop asked Huxley, with a smile, whether it was through his grandfather or his grandmother that he claimed descent from an ape. Huxley replied, as I heard it, that he would not be ashamed to have an ape for a grandfather, but that he would be ashamed to be connected with a man who used great gifts to obscure the truth. Accounts differ as to the exact words. Lady Brewster fainted. I do not think that anyone's mind was changed that day; but it was clear which way the young men were leaning.

Darwin said almost nothing in the Origin about mankind, except one sentence: that light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history. Four years ago, in The Descent of Man, he said the rest: that man is descended from an ape-like ancestor, probably in Africa, and that our moral sense, our affections and our intellect differ from those of the animals in degree, not in kind.

The Encyclopaedia of the future tells me that Darwin's theory has become the foundation of all the sciences of life. The mechanism of inheritance, which Darwin did not understand, was discovered first by an Austrian monk named Gregor Mendel, who has published his experiments on peas in an obscure journal in Brno, which nobody has read, and later, in the twentieth century, in the structure of a substance within every cell, which carries the instructions of inheritance in a code, and which the men of the future can now read and even rewrite. Every discovery since, the Encyclopaedia says, has confirmed the common descent of all living things. Darwin will die, I learn, in eighteen eighty-two, and be buried in Westminster Abbey, a few feet from Newton.

He wrote at the end of the Origin a sentence that I think the most beautiful in the scientific literature of our language. There is grandeur in this view of life, that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved. Whether that view leaves room for God, Darwin himself was uncertain, and I shall not pretend to settle what he could not. I will say only that I have found the grandeur real.
